about: Daily Tortuga Scan notes. Add a new object at the start of reports[]. Date is the local day in America/Los_Angeles. Every item needs a real source URL. See README.md.
editorial: Dial down FDA recall items unless they clearly affect people using this app, for example a product sold in Nevada or a nationally relevant clean-living product. Prefer clean-product launches, studies, and clean-living policy news.

reports.title: Wednesday, November 18, 2026
reports.dek: An organic puffed cereal heading to Nevada Whole Foods stores, a Clean Label Project–certified electrolyte mix, seed-oil-free bone broth marinara at Sprouts, an award for a steadier natural spirulina blue, a Virginia Tech brain study on ultra-processed diets in young adults, a heart failure link to ultra-processed food, the White House pulling its FDA commissioner pick, and a consumer group’s push for a harm-based ultra-processed food definition.

items.headline: Good Grains organic puffed cereal heads to Whole Foods, including Nevada
items.summary: In a November 17 release, Good Grains said its organic puffed cereals (Corn, Honey, and Cinnamon Puffs) will expand from about 630 stores to close to 2,000 in early 2027, starting in January at 132 Whole Foods Market locations in states including Nevada, plus 386 select Target stores, Fresh Thyme, Harris Teeter, and ShopRite. It is already in about 500 Sprouts stores. The brand says the cereals are USDA Organic, made from organic khorasan wheat and organic corn, sweetened only with honey and a little monk fruit, with no seed oils or artificial ingredients, and certified glyphosate residue-free and Non-UPF Verified by WISEcode. It also says box prices drop to $5.99 to $6.99 on January 1. Those are the brand’s claims; Tortuga hasn’t graded a barcode yet.

items.headline: Puori launches a batch-tested electrolyte mix with no added sugar
items.summary: Prepared Foods reported on November 17 that supplement maker Puori launched Electrolytes+, a lemon electrolyte powder made with magnesium bisglycinate, potassium citrate, and unrefined Himalayan salt, with no added sugar or artificial ingredients. Each sachet lists 600 mg sodium, 300 mg potassium, and 60 mg magnesium. Puori says every batch is tested and certified by the Clean Label Project for more than 200 contaminants, including heavy metals and pesticides, and that you can look up your batch’s results with the QR code on the pack. It’s sold on puori.com.

items.headline: SAUZ and Kettle & Fire team up on a seed-oil-free bone broth marinara
items.summary: NOSH’s November 13 new-products roundup says SAUZ and bone broth brand Kettle & Fire launched a marinara made with bone broth and California-grown tomatoes, in Chicken (Sautéed Red Pepper & Herb) and Beef (Caramelized Onion & Herb). Each 16 oz. jar has 16 g protein, and both are described as gluten-free, seed-oil-free, and made without added sugar. It’s rolling out to Kroger, Sprouts, and select Texas Costco stores, plus getsauz.com. The same roundup notes Nowhere Bakery’s new grain-free pizza dough mix made without seed oils or gums. Check your local shelf before you go.

items.headline: A steadier natural spirulina blue wins an award at Fi Europe
items.summary: GNT, the maker of EXBERRY colors, won the Plant-based Innovation Award at Fi Europe in Frankfurt on November 17 for a technology meant to keep spirulina’s natural blue stable in acidic drinks, through heat processing, and on the shelf. Spirulina blue usually breaks down in those conditions, which is one reason drinks still lean on synthetic Blue No. 1. The coverage gives no performance figures. It’s an ingredient for manufacturers, not something you’ll buy at the store, but it could help brands drop synthetic blues.

items.headline: Two weeks of ultra-processed food changed how young adults’ brains responded to a milkshake
items.summary: Virginia Tech researchers ran a feeding trial with 22 people ages 18 to 25. Each ate a diet with 81% of calories from ultra-processed food for two weeks and, after a break, a diet with none, with the two diets matched for macronutrients, fiber, added sugar, sodium, and calories. In the 18-to-21 group, the ultra-processed diet was tied to a weaker response to a milkshake in the orbitofrontal cortex, a brain area involved in food reward and decision-making; the 22-to-25 group showed no significant change. The paper is in the journal Obesity. It’s a small trial and the age findings are exploratory, so the researchers say more work is needed.

items.headline: More ultra-processed food is linked to a higher risk of heart failure
items.summary: A study of 6,531 U.S. adults ages 45 to 84 in the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis, published November 16 in JACC: Heart Failure, found that each extra daily serving of ultra-processed food was tied to about a 5% higher risk of developing heart failure in the main model. The link was driven mainly by the type of heart failure called HFpEF, and people in the top 80% of intake had more than twice the HFpEF risk of the lowest 20%. Waist-to-height ratio accounted for about half of the link. It’s observational, so it shows a link, not proof of cause.

alsoSee.name: HCPLive interview with the lead author

items.headline: White House pulls Heidi Overton’s nomination to run the FDA
items.summary: The White House withdrew Heidi Overton’s nomination for FDA commissioner on the night of November 17, a day before a Senate committee vote. Some MAHA supporters had opposed her, saying she wouldn’t push back hard enough on corporate interests. Kyle Diamantas, the agency’s former food chief, stays on as acting commissioner, and no new nominee had been named. Big food rules are still open, including a proposal to make GRAS notifications mandatory, with comments due December 9.

items.headline: CSPI calls for a harm-based definition of ultra-processed food
items.summary: In a piece updated November 17, the Center for Science in the Public Interest says the federal ultra-processed food definition is still stuck at the White House budget office after more than a dozen industry meetings. CSPI argues for a harm-based definition that targets foods high in sodium, added sugar, or saturated fat, processed meats, sweetened drinks, refined carbs, and additives tied to serious harms like cancer, rather than relying only on the Nova system. It also warns that new “non-UPF” labels can be healthwashing without a clear standard. This is an advocacy group’s position, not a rule.
items.sourceName: Center for Science in the Public Interest

reports.title: Tuesday, November 17, 2026
reports.dek: Date-based sour candy, a four-ingredient fruit granola at Target, nitrate-free fungi deli slices at Sprouts, a beet red pitched for candy, a UK blood-marker study on ultra-processed diets, a New York additive ban on the governor’s desk, a renewed White House push to define ultra-processed food, and a regenerative farming pledge from 14 big food companies.

items.headline: Actually Fruit’s Super Loops: sour candy cut from organic dates
items.summary: In a November 14 release, Boulder-based Actually Fruit said its Super Loops are on shelves nationwide at Whole Foods Market, Natural Grocers, and Amazon in Sour Strawberry Lemonade, Sour Blue Raspberry, and Sour Watermelon. The company lists five ingredients (organic dates, organic flavor, organic coconut glycerin, malic acid, citric acid) and says the dates are sliced into rings, with no puree, syrup, or gelatin. The label it cites shows 0 g added sugar, 3 g fiber, and 80 calories per 30 g serving. Dates still carry natural sugar, so this is a cleaner candy swap, not a free pass.

items.headline: That’s it. brings Fruitola fruit granola to Target
items.summary: Netty reported on November 16 that That’s it. launched Fruitola Fruit Granola at Target stores nationwide in Banana, Cinnamon, Strawberry, and Blueberry. The company says it is made with four ingredients and no added sugar, is gluten-free, and has 16 g plant-based protein and 7 g fiber per bowl. Those are the brand’s own claims. Tortuga hasn’t graded a barcode yet.

items.headline: Prime Roots Safe Slice deli cuts roll out at Sprouts nationwide
items.summary: Mass Market Retailers reported on November 10 that Prime Roots is rolling out Safe Slice, ready-to-eat deli slices made from fungi protein, at Sprouts Farmers Market stores nationwide, timed to the No Nitrates November campaign. The company says the line has no added nitrates and no hidden nitrate sources like celery powder, and is gluten-free, soy-free, and free of the top nine allergens, with turkey, ham, salami, and roast beef styles. Sprouts has Las Vegas and Henderson stores, but check your local shelf before you go.

items.headline: A crystal beet red aimed at candy and dairy debuts at Fi Europe
items.summary: California Natural Color said it is introducing Pure Red Beet, a beet-derived red in its crystal format, at Fi Europe in Frankfurt, November 17 to 19. It is pitched for dairy, candy, and plant-based foods. The supplier says the crystals are 5 to 10 times more concentrated than liquid colors. It’s one more plant-based option for brands moving off synthetic reds like Red 40. These are supplier claims, and it’s an ingredient for manufacturers, not something you’ll buy at the store.

items.headline: UK study finds a blood ‘signature’ of ultra-processed diets
items.summary: UCL and Imperial College London researchers used Whitehall II data on more than 6,000 UK adults followed for up to 20 years and measured 233 blood metabolites. The pattern tied to ultra-processed diets had more unhealthy fats and less omega-3, and a minimally processed diet showed the opposite. The researchers say this pattern explained 43% to 51% of the diet’s link to heart disease and type 2 diabetes, even after accounting for sugar, fat, and salt. They also say more research is needed. The paper came out in BMC Medicine in July; UCL publicized it on November 4. It’s observational, so it shows a link, not proof of cause.

items.headline: New York bill banning Red 3, potassium bromate, and propylparaben reaches Hochul
items.summary: The Food Safety and Chemical Disclosure Act (S1239-F / A1556-G) went to New York Gov. Kathy Hochul on November 13. It would ban food made with Red No. 3, potassium bromate, or propylparaben. It would also make New York the first state to require companies to report ingredients they have self-declared safe (self-affirmed GRAS) to a public state database, with small businesses exempt. Industry groups are urging a veto over costs. As of these reports, she had neither signed nor vetoed it. The ban wouldn’t start right away; the bill builds in phase-in time.

items.headline: White House renews its push for a federal ultra-processed food definition
items.summary: Politico reported on November 13, citing two people familiar with the talks, that the administration is again pushing to finalize a federal definition of ultra-processed food after progress stalled last month. Meetings with officials and industry have picked up since Stephen Miller became chief of staff. MAHA supporters see a definition as the first step toward labeling. No text has been published yet, so nothing changes on labels for now.

items.headline: Fourteen food companies sign a regenerative farming pledge
items.summary: On November 17, companies including Nestlé, McDonald’s, Mars, Danone, and McCain Foods, plus retailers like Waitrose, Marks & Spencer, Lidl GB, and Aldi Süd, signed the Regen Compact, led by the Circular Bioeconomy Alliance. They commit to building more regenerative agriculture into how they operate and to tracking progress in a farmer-led way. Reports say each company sets its own actions, with no shared numeric target. It’s a pledge, not a certification, so it doesn’t make any one product regenerative or organic.

items.headline: Consumer Reports tests 21 kids’ vitamins against their labels
items.summary: Consumer Reports tested 21 children’s vitamins, including Flintstones, Hiya, Nature Made, and SmartyPants, and says every product had at least one nutrient amount that differed from its label. The article (published November 10, updated November 12) has the brand-by-brand results and also covers heavy metals. Tortuga isn’t repeating figures here. Read CR’s tables before you buy.

reports.title: Monday, November 16, 2026
reports.dek: A certified avocado oil lands at Walmart, Crunchmaster says its crackers are now seed-oil-free certified, a radish red is pitched in place of Red 40, two papers look at ultra-processed food, glyphosate-residue-free sales are reported at $2.8 billion, and FDA confirms Orange B stays off sausage casings.

items.headline: Pompeian launches a certified avocado oil, only at Walmart
items.summary: On November 12, Pompeian said it is selling Pompeian 100% Pure Avocado Oil in a 16-ounce bottle, only at Walmart. The company says the oil is pressed from avocado flesh, naturally refined, and Seed Oil Free Certified by the Seed Oil Free Alliance after a check against that group’s standard. The same release gives two smoke-point figures: up to 500°F in the story and up to 520°F in the bullet list. Tortuga is leaving both numbers on the page rather than picking one. A seed-oil-free certification is one check. It is not a lab test of every bottle on the shelf.

items.headline: Crunchmaster says every cracker and crisp is seed-oil-free certified
items.summary: Crunchmaster’s own page says every cracker and crisp manufactured on or after November 1, 2026, is Seed Oil Free Certified by the Seed Oil Free Alliance, and that the seal is expected on packs in early to mid-2027 even though the certification is already in effect. The page says the oils used are avocado oil and olive oil, reviewed and lab-tested for purity by the Alliance, and that whole seeds in the crackers are not the thing the seal is about. The company also says the certification is not a medical or disease-prevention claim, and that the crackers are still gluten-free. A certification is the certifier’s standard, not a Tortuga grade of a barcode.

items.headline: Oterra pitches a radish powder as a Red 40 stand-in
items.summary: theFutureofFood.org reported on November 13 that Oterra launched ColorFruit Red Radish Powder on November 12, from Mount Pleasant, Wisconsin, and is aiming it at cereals, snacks, baked goods, and frostings. Oterra says the color stays vivid at neutral pH and holds above 350°F through baking and extrusion. The article says those performance claims are the company’s, with no independent test data, no customers, and no price in the announcement. Oterra, citing Innova Market Insights, said about 70% of U.S. food and beverage launches with synthetic colors in the 12 months ending October 2026 contained Red 40. A separate fermentation red Oterra is developing with Debut is not on the market and still needs FDA approval.

items.headline: Glyphosate Residue Free certified sales reported at $2.8 billion
items.summary: Where the Food Comes From, writing on November 16 from a Detox Project report, says SPINS checkout data put U.S. and Canadian sales of Glyphosate Residue Free certified products at $2.8 billion, up 180% from the year before. The same piece says a SPINS report covering the third quarter of 2025 had the market at $1 billion. It also says the Detox Project’s newer CleanScan program, a QR code for heavy-metal and pesticide results, has reached $120 million in certified-product sales. The article describes the Glyphosate Residue Free rule as regular tests by an ISO 17025 lab and no glyphosate down to usual government limits of detection, often 0.01 ppm. That is the certification’s bar, not a new public test of one jar in this catalog.

items.headline: UK nutrient scores miss a lot of ultra-processed foods, a BMJ Medicine paper says
items.summary: FoodNavigator’s November 12 report on a BMJ Medicine study says researchers scored 1,898 UK products with five nutrient profiling models. The Food Standards Agency model called 57.6% unhealthy. Traffic-light labels called 48.2% unhealthy. Three newer models built from the Eatwell Guide called 91.5%, 94.9%, and 98.7% of the ultra-processed products unhealthy. FoodNavigator says a 2018 revision of the agency model, due in January 2027, still flagged 25 to 35 percent fewer processed and ultra-processed products than the most conservative of those new models. This is a UK shelf study, not a lab test of a U.S. barcode.

items.headline: EWG: most papers criticizing the Nova ultra-processed label had industry ties
items.summary: On November 12, EWG described an American Journal of Public Health study of 69 papers, published from 2009 through 2025, that questioned the Nova ultra-processed-food system or pointed to benefits of ultra-processed food. The papers had 232 authors. EWG says 91% of the articles had at least one author with a food-industry tie, about 69% of the authors had such a connection, and for 71% of those authors the tie was not disclosed in the paper and showed up only in a search of public records. Arguments for ultra-processed food showed up in two-fifths of articles with direct industry ties and in 17% of articles with no apparent industry ties. EWG also notes that an industry tie does not by itself throw out a study.

items.headline: FDA confirms Orange B is no longer allowed on hot-dog casings
items.summary: A Federal Register notice dated November 13 confirms the September 8, 2026 effective date of FDA’s July 23 order repealing the color-additive listing for Orange B on the casings or surfaces of frankfurters and sausages. FDA says no objections and no hearing requests were filed by the August 24 deadline, so the repeal stands. This is a dye listing that had already been pulled, not a new recall of a product on a Nevada shelf.

reports.title: Tuesday, November 10, 2026
reports.dek: FDA pulls three solvents from food-color production, a House bill would ban every certified dye plus BHA, BHT, and TBHQ, seed-oil-free sales hit $1 billion, and two new launches skip seed oils.

items.headline: FDA revokes cancer-linked solvents used to make some food colors
items.summary: FDA is ending two remaining color-additive uses for methylene chloride and related solvents. One was methylene chloride as a thinner in the inks used to mark fruit and vegetables, which consumer groups including EWG and the Environmental Defense Fund had petitioned against. The other covers methylene chloride, ethylene dichloride, and trichloroethylene in making annatto extract, paprika oleoresin, and turmeric oleoresin, which the color makers’ own trade group asked FDA to drop. FDA acted under the Delaney Clause, which bars ingested color additives shown to cause cancer in people or animals. The revocations take effect January 11, 2027. Annatto, paprika, and turmeric colors stay allowed; only these solvents go.

items.headline: House bills would ban all certified dyes and BHA, BHT, and TBHQ
items.summary: Rep. Nancy Mace introduced two bills. H.R. 10936 (October 29) would have HHS treat every batch-certified color additive, like Red 40 and Yellow 5, as unsafe in food, drugs, devices, and cosmetics two years after it became law. H.R. 10913 (October 26) would make food containing any BHA, BHT, or TBHQ adulterated, also after two years. Both sit in the House Energy and Commerce Committee with no hearing or vote scheduled, so nothing changes yet. FDA’s current push to remove the six remaining synthetic dyes is still voluntary, with an end-of-2027 target, and Red 3 is out of food after January 15, 2027. Tortuga already docks BHA, BHT, and TBHQ.

items.headline: Seed-oil-free product sales reach $1 billion
items.summary: Morning Brew, citing a Bloomberg report, says sales of products labeled seed-oil-free rose 72 percent to about $1 billion over the past year. Health brands and big snack makers, including PepsiCo and Utz, are adding chips and snacks cooked in alternatives such as beef tallow. A seed-oil-free claim is still only one check: scan the rest of the label for gums, natural flavors, and conventional glyphosate-prone crops.

items.headline: Stellar Snacks bakes a Pretzel Braids line with olive oil, only at Sprouts
items.summary: Stellar Snacks, based in Carson City, Nevada, launched Pretzel Braids Baked with Olive Oil, a six-flavor seed-oil-free line sold only at Sprouts Farmers Market nationwide. Two flavors are new, Elote Loco and Spicy Flame, alongside Maui Monk, Bold & Herby, Cinnamon Dolce, and French Dijon. The original braids at Target, Kroger, and Costco are a separate line, so check which bag you grab. Pretzels are wheat, so look for organic flour on the label before calling it a full pass.
items.sourceName: Recipes ’n Cooking, citing the brand’s press release

items.headline: Incredifulls rolls out frozen PB&J cups made without seed oils
items.summary: Incredifulls, the Pizza Cupcake brand, is launching Paw Patrol Peanut Butter & Jelly Cups nationally: peanut butter and jelly baked inside a sourdough-brioche crust, sold frozen in boxes of four for a suggested $5.99 to $6.99. The company says they are made without seed oils, artificial colors, or high-fructose corn syrup, with 5 g of protein each. We haven’t seen the full ingredient list yet, so sugar and flour quality are unknown until it’s scanned.

items.headline: Pumpkin seeds and pumpkin seed oil didn’t beat a plain low-cholesterol diet
items.summary: A randomized trial in the Irish Journal of Medical Science followed 89 overweight adults with high blood lipids for four weeks on a low-cholesterol diet, adding 30 g a day of pumpkin seeds, 15 g a day of pumpkin seed oil, or nothing. Cholesterol, LDL, and liver enzymes fell in all three groups. Triglycerides dropped only in the two pumpkin groups, but the difference between groups wasn’t statistically significant. The authors say more research is needed. It’s small and short, so the takeaway is that the diet change did most of the work.

items.headline: Fresh To You breakfast biscuit sandwiches recalled for Listeria
items.summary: Fresh & Ready Foods of Renton, Washington, is recalling 2,414 Fresh To You Sausage, Egg & Cheese Biscuit Sandwiches (4.6 oz, UPC 8 405493 0168 4, Fresh Thru 11/07 to 11/19). The biscuit came from a CH Guenther & Son recall. They went to break rooms, vending machines, and cafeterias in Oregon and Washington only, so Nevada shelves aren’t on the list. No illnesses reported. Don’t eat it; the company offers refunds.

items.headline: Mexico drops Red 3 and starts a new food-additive rulebook this month
items.summary: Mexico’s Health Ministry removed Red 3 (erythrosine) from foods, drinks, and supplements in May, giving companies 24 months to reformulate. A separate agreement replacing its 2012 additive rules starts this month, with sources giving dates from November 13 to late November. Some colorants get numeric limits for the first time, and additives must be listed by name on labels.

reports.title: Monday, November 9, 2026
reports.dek: First Tortuga Scan daily note. Recalls and public lab alerts from the past week, in our words. Older studies — avocado oil, cocoa metals, infant rice arsenic — are filed under Lab tests, not as today’s headlines.

items.headline: Brad’s kale chips recalled after thallium testing
items.summary: Snack Right Super Foods, which sells Brad’s Raw Chips, is recalling about 25,000 bags of Brad’s Plant Based Crunchy Kale (2 oz) and Veggie Chips Kale (3 oz). FDA posted the notice on November 3. The chips went out through KeHE and UNFI between October and December 2025, and best-by dates run into February 2027. California’s health department tested store samples in the Sacramento area after one person had high thallium, and FDA then told the company. The notice says drying removes about 85 to 90 percent of the water and concentrates metal already in the kale. It does not publish a thallium number. The company is not giving refunds. Don’t eat the listed lots.

items.headline: Once Upon a Farm recalls Tractor Wheels toddler bars
items.summary: Once Upon a Farm is recalling every lot and flavor of Tractor Wheels Organic Toddler Soft-Baked Bars. FDA published the company notice on November 2; the company dated it October 30. The firm says three choking complaints were reported to FDA and that no injuries have been reported to the company. FDA’s own advisory, updated November 3, says it has several reports of toddlers about 1.5 to 2.5 years old whose airway was fully blocked, and that some incidents needed emergency care and hospital observation. Both say the bar can turn into a dry, sticky mass when chewed. Other Once Upon a Farm products are not part of this recall. The company says it is reformulating. Don’t serve the bars; take them back or throw them out.

items.headline: USDA alert: Betterballen snacks left sesame and fish off the label
items.summary: On November 6, USDA’s food safety service issued a public health alert for frozen Betterballen Bami Rolls, Saté Kroketten, and Bitterballen. The labels don’t say sesame. The beef bitterballen also contain anchovy in the Worcestershire sauce and don’t say fish. A recall was not asked for because the products are no longer for sale, but some may still be in freezers. They were made October 15, 16, and 27, 2026, sold online by Lowlands House, and may have been sold at a festival and farmers market in Greer, South Carolina. No illnesses were confirmed. Throw them out or take them back.

items.headline: FDA lists Wise Wife cinnamon at 2.118 ppm lead
items.summary: On November 4, FDA added a Wise Wife ground cinnamon to its public alert after the Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station measured 2.118 ppm lead. The jar is 110 g, UPC 0688474302754, best before April 25, 2027, and was recalled October 29. The same FDA table lists an older Wise Wife UPC at 2.49 ppm. FDA says those levels are much lower than the 2,270 to 5,110 ppm lead in cinnamon from the 2023 WanaBana applesauce recall, and still says to throw the listed cinnamon out. Figures and links are in Lab tests.
